questions.question: Which of the following statements about the action potential are correct?
correct: The action potential is generated by depolarization and repolarization of the cell.
In the resting state, the cell has a negative membrane potential of approximately -70 mV.
During depolarization, voltage-dependent sodium channels open and Na+ enters rapidly, making the interior positive (approx. +30 mV, 1 ms).
During repolarization, sodium channels close and potassium channels open; K+ exits the cell, restoring the negative internal polarity in approx. 1-2 ms.
The sodium-potassium pump redistributes the ions (expels Na+ and takes in K+), returning the cell to its resting state.
wrong: In the resting state, the cell has a positive membrane potential of approximately +70 mV.
During depolarization, K+ enters the cell rapidly and makes the interior negative.
The action potential of cardiac muscle usually lasts only about 1 ms.
The sodium-potassium pump works by facilitated diffusion, with no energy consumption.
Once the threshold is reached, the cell can immediately generate a new action potential during repolarization.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about action potential duration are correct?
correct: In nerve and muscle cells, repolarization is so fast that the action potential appears as a spike with a total duration of only 1 ms.
The whole action potential wave lasts approximately 3-5 ms.
The action potential of the heart muscle usually lasts between 150 and 300 ms.
When several cells are excited simultaneously, their action potentials sum up.
Depolarization of the heart muscle cells generates electric potential variations detectable at the level of the limb extremities.
wrong: The action potential of the heart muscle usually lasts about 1-2 ms.
The whole action potential wave lasts approximately 150-300 ms.
In nerve cells, the action potential spike lasts about 150 ms.
When several cells are excited simultaneously, their action potentials cancel each other out.
Repolarization in nerve and muscle cells takes 150-300 ms.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about biosignals are correct?
correct: The biosignals most often measured are ECG, EMG and EEG.
The parameters usually measured are the amplitude and the frequency.
The heart is a source of electric signal with amplitudes of 100 µV ... 4 mV and a frequency spectrum of 0.1 Hz ... 100 Hz.
The brain is an electric signal source with amplitudes of 10 µV ... 100 µV and a spectrum of 0.1 Hz ... 100 Hz.
The neuromuscular system is a source of electric signal with amplitudes of 100 µV ... 4 mV and a spectrum of 5 Hz ... 2 kHz.
wrong: The biosignals most often measured are ECG, EMG and ERG.
The parameters usually measured are the period and the polarity only.
The heart signal spectrum is 5 Hz ... 2 kHz.
The brain signal amplitude is 100 µV ... 4 mV.
EMG is measured with an electrode with contact lens.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the human body as an electrical resistance and the effects of current through the body are correct?
correct: 1,000,000 ohms is considered the maximum electrical resistance of the human body under ideal coupling conditions.
Once the current manages to pass through the insulating layer of the skin, what matters is only the intensity - that is what kills us or merely tickles us.
1 mA is the threshold of sensation.
5 mA is the accepted maximum harmless current intensity.
The maximum safe current with a frequency between 0 Hz ... 1 kHz applied to the cardiac muscle is only 10 µA.
wrong: 100,000 ohms is considered the maximum electrical resistance of the human body.
Once current passes through the skin, the voltage is what determines the danger.
1 mA is the threshold of ventricular fibrillation.
50 mA is the accepted maximum harmless current intensity.
The maximum safe current applied to the cardiac muscle is 10 mA.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the effects of 50 Hz current (electric shock) applied between the two arms for 1 s are correct?
correct: 10 mA ... 20 mA is the threshold of permanent muscle contraction.
50 mA causes pain, possible fainting, mechanical injury; cardiac and respiratory activities continue.
100 mA ... 300 mA causes ventricular fibrillation; respiration continues.
6 A causes temporary respiratory paralysis and persistent myocardial contraction followed by a normal rhythm; burns if current density is high.
The effects of the current are maximal around the 50 Hz mains frequency.
wrong: 10 mA ... 20 mA is the threshold of sensation.
50 mA causes ventricular fibrillation.
100 mA ... 300 mA is the accepted maximum harmless current.
6 A causes permanent respiratory paralysis.
For frequencies above 200 Hz, the current still has a stimulator effect.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about electrodes are correct?
correct: The human body is a quasi-electrolyte, in which conduction is ionic, while in a metal electrode conduction is electronic.
At the interface, phenomena transform ionic conduction into electronic conduction and vice versa.
Wet electrodes (metal applied to the skin through an electrolyte) are preferred over dry electrodes.
Active electrodes have a pre-amplification module immediately after the conductive material between skin and electrode.
Surface electrodes usually use a conductive gel to reduce the skin-electrode impedance.
wrong: Dry electrodes (metal applied directly on the skin) are always preferred over wet electrodes.
In the human body, conduction is electronic, not ionic.
Active electrodes have the pre-amplification module far away from the skin-electrode interface.
Single-use surface electrodes contain no conductive gel.
At the skin-electrode interface there is no charge transfer between ionic and electronic conduction.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the equivalent circuit of surface electrodes are correct?
correct: The biological channel represents the areas of the organism that the biosignal (Et) traverses to reach the body surface.
The skin has reduced and especially variable electrical conductivity (Rp) and also has a capacitive component.

The skin-electrode interface is the most restrictive crossing zone, equivalent to a voltage source called the half-cell potential Ei, in series with a parallel grouping Ci, Ri, in parallel with a leakage resistance Rfi.
The half-cell potential is a disturbing signal source and must be reduced as much as possible.
The electrode has resistive behavior (Re) and the differential input of the amplifier has resistive behavior (Rd).
wrong: The skin has high and constant electrical conductivity.
The half-cell potential is a useful signal that must be amplified.
The skin-electrode interface is the least restrictive crossing zone.
The leakage resistance Rfi is in series with the half-cell potential.
The biological channel has no influence on the measured biosignal.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the requirements imposed on electrodes are correct?
correct: They must not influence the biological process.
They must ensure optimal uptake of the useful signal and rejection of artifacts from the biological channel and external electrical disturbances.
They must have stability over time of characteristics under mechanical, physical and chemical disturbances.
They must be robust, easy, non-intrusive for the patient, with simple and fast handling.
They must have low cost.
wrong: They may influence the biological process as long as the signal is amplified later.
Rejecting artifacts is optional, since the buffer stage removes all noise.
Stability over time under disturbances is not required.
High cost is acceptable for implantable electrodes only.
Patient comfort is not a design requirement.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the protection stage and EMC standards are correct?
correct: I/O and power supply pins that connect an electronic device to the outside world are a major source of failures due to EMI and ESD.
The standard IEC/EN 60601-1-2 defines the type of interference that medical devices must withstand.
According to the standard, interference must not cause failure in diagnosis or treatment, false alarms, or unintended activation of operations.
ESD immunity is tested per EN 61000-4-2 at ±6 kV contact and ±8 kV air.
Radiated RF immunity is tested per EN 61000-4-3 at 3 V/m from 80 MHz to 2.5 GHz.
wrong: The standard IEC/EN 60601-1-2 defines only the mechanical requirements of medical devices.
ESD immunity is tested at ±60 kV contact and ±80 kV air.
Radiated RF immunity is tested at 3 V/m from 150 kHz to 80 MHz.
Interference is allowed to cause false alarms as long as they are visible.
EMI stands for Electronic Medical Interference.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about transient voltage suppressors (TVS) are correct?
correct: TVS components clamp the transient overvoltage to an acceptable voltage level.
When the voltage is below the threshold, an ideal TVS should be in an open-circuit state.
When the voltage exceeds the threshold, an ideal TVS immediately goes into a short-circuit state with unlimited current flow.
A silicon diode has a threshold of 0.7 V and a germanium diode 0.3 V.
A varistor with metal oxide (MOV) has a threshold range of 5 V - 1.8 kV, and a gas discharge tube (GDT) 60 V - 5 kV.
wrong: When the voltage is below the threshold, an ideal TVS should be in a short-circuit state.
A silicon diode has a threshold of 7 V.
A Zener diode has a threshold range of 0.1 - 0.5 V.
A gas discharge tube has a threshold range of 5 V - 60 V.
TVS components are used to amplify the transient overvoltage.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the buffer stage are correct?
correct: The noise introduced by the buffer stage must be much smaller than the measured input signal.
The input impedance must be much larger than the source impedance.
The maximum admissible overvoltage depends on the characteristics of the protection circuit and the limiting device.
The buffer must support the input dynamic range plus all permitted interference without modifying the source signal beyond the prescribed limits.
If the signal shape is significant, as in ECG, the buffer stage must have a linear phase property: all frequency components in the passband must have the same time delay.
wrong: The input impedance must be much smaller than the source impedance.
The buffer stage must not add any noise limit regarding the measured signal.
For ECG-like signals, the buffer must introduce attenuation at specific frequencies where the source signal is significant.
The buffer stage is optional when the protection circuit is present.
The buffer stage may modify the input signal through nonlinear performance as long as it amplifies.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about analog vs digital signal processing are correct?
correct: Digital signals are processed more easily than their analog counterparts because operations are performed on values discrete, sampled in time and quantized in amplitude.
Digital signals do not suffer noise degradation as long as the noise does not exceed certain limits.
Analog signals have continuous amplitude-time values and their processing requires that the waveform not be significantly distorted.
Noise cannot be eliminated in analog processing, so its interference must be limited by careful design choices.
Analog circuit design is much more critical, and analog circuits cannot always be replaced by digital processing.
wrong: Analog signals are processed more easily than digital ones.
Digital signals suffer noise degradation even below the noise limits.
Noise can be completely eliminated in analog processing.
Analog circuit design is less critical than digital design.
Analog circuits can always be replaced by digital processing.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the operational amplifier summing circuit are correct?
correct: Compared to the voltage follower, adding several input resistors at the input, each equal to the initial input resistance Rin, gives an inverting summing amplifier.
The inverting summing amplifier is also called a 'voltage summer' circuit.
It subtracts rather than sums the input voltages.
It is built around an operational amplifier with external resistive feedback.
It is one of the circuits commonly used in forming and processing biomedical signals.
wrong: Adding input resistors to a voltage follower gives a non-inverting summing amplifier.
The summing amplifier adds the input voltages without changing their sign.
The summing amplifier requires no feedback resistor.
It cannot be used with biomedical signals.
It amplifies only a single input signal.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the differential amplifier are correct?
correct: The differential amplifier is a voltage subtractor circuit that produces an output voltage proportional to the difference of two input voltages applied to the inverting and non-inverting terminals.
A standard op-amp has two inputs, inverting and non-inverting, and signals can be connected to both at the same time.
Unlike the summing amplifier which adds the input voltages, the differential amplifier subtracts them.
It is used to amplify the difference between two signals while rejecting what they have in common.
It is one of the basic circuits used in biomedical signal processing.
wrong: The differential amplifier produces an output proportional to the sum of the two input voltages.
A standard op-amp has only one usable input for amplification.
The differential amplifier amplifies a single input signal referenced to ground only.
It cannot reject common-mode signals.
It is not used in medical instrumentation.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the instrumentation amplifier are correct?
correct: Instrumentation amplifiers are differential amplifiers with very high gain, high input impedance and a single-ended output.
They are used mainly to amplify very small differential signals from voltage stamps to biosignals.
Unlike standard op-amps, they have an internal feedback resistor effectively isolated from their input terminals because the input signal is applied to two differential inputs V1 and V2.
They have a very good common-mode rejection ratio CMRR (zero output when V1 = V2).
CMRR quantifies the ability to reject common-mode signals, i.e. those appearing simultaneously and in phase on both inputs.
wrong: Instrumentation amplifiers have low input impedance and a differential output.
They use an external feedback resistor between output and input to set the gain.
They have poor common-mode rejection.
CMRR is the measure of amplification of common-mode signals.
They are used mainly for large single-ended signals.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the internal structure of the instrumentation amplifier are correct?
correct: The two non-inverting amplifiers A1 and A2 form a differential input stage acting as buffers with a gain of 1 + 2R2/R1 for differential input signals.
A1 and A2 have unity gain for common-mode input signals.
The differential gain of the circuit can be varied by simply changing the value of R1.
When a common-mode voltage is applied, no current flows through R1, so A1 and A2 work as buffers.
The output of the differential amplifier A3 is the difference between its two inputs (V2 - V1), amplified by the gain of A3 which can be one (assuming R3 = R4).
wrong: The input stage gain is 2R2/R1 without the '+1' term.
A1 and A2 have a gain of 1 + 2R2/R1 for common-mode signals.
The gain is varied by changing R2 only, R1 stays fixed.
Common-mode voltage causes current to flow through R1.
A3 output is the sum (V1 + V2) of its inputs.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the isolation amplifier are correct?
correct: Instruments applied in the presence of a common-mode voltage without an isolation barrier allow ground currents to flow, leading in the best case to a noisy measured signal and in the worst case to destruction of the instrument.
Isolation amplifiers are used in medical instruments to isolate the patient from the leakage current of the power supply.
Isolation can be realized with inductive coupling (transformers).
Isolation can be realized with optic coupling (LED emitter and photodiode or phototransistor receiver, in the optical or infrared domain).

Isolation can be realized with capacitive coupling (preamplified signal transformed into two complementary medium-frequency signals transferred through two capacitors acting as an isolation barrier, then demodulated with a PLL loop) and by radio telemetry (WiFi, Bluetooth).
wrong: Without an isolation barrier, ground currents cannot flow.
Isolation amplifiers are used to increase the gain of the biosignal.
Optic coupling uses a transformer.
Capacitive coupling transfers the signal through resistors acting as a barrier.
Isolation amplifiers connect the patient directly to the mains ground.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about filters in general are correct?
correct: Filters are networks that process signals in a frequency-dependent manner.
Filters can be used to separate signals, passing those of interest and attenuating unwanted frequencies.
In low-frequency applications (up to 100 kHz), passive filters are generally built using simple RC networks.
At higher frequencies (above 100 kHz), filters are usually made of RLC components.
Filters are divided into two distinct types: active and passive filters.
wrong: Filters process signals independently of frequency.
Up to 100 kHz, passive filters are usually RLC networks.
Above 100 kHz, filters are usually RC networks.
There is only one type of filter: the active one.
Filters amplify all frequencies equally.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about passive vs active filters are correct?
correct: In a passive filter, the output signal amplitude is smaller than the input signal, so passive RC filters attenuate the signal and have a gain smaller than one.
The main disadvantage of passive filters is that the output amplitude is smaller than the input and the load impedance affects the filter characteristics.
In multi-stage passive filters, this signal loss called attenuation can become very severe.
Active filters are filtering circuits that use an operational amplifier as the main amplifying device together with resistors and capacitors.
Active filters draw power from an external power supply and use it to increase or amplify the output signal.
wrong: Passive filters have a gain greater than one.
The load impedance does not affect passive filter characteristics.
Active filters do not need an external power supply.
Active filters always attenuate the signal like passive ones.
Attenuation in multi-stage passive filters becomes negligible.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the active low-pass filter are correct?
correct: In the active low-pass filter, the capacitor is moved from the op-amp input to the feedback circuit, in parallel with R2.
The parallel combination of C and R2 sets the -3 dB point as before, but allows the amplifier gain to decrease to infinity beyond the cutoff frequency.
The DC gain is set by the standard inverting formula -R2/R1 (e.g. = 10).
At a sufficiently high frequency, the gain reaches unity (0 dB) as the amplifier effectively becomes a follower, so the gain equation becomes 1 + 0/R1 = 1.
A second-order active low-pass filter is obtained by simply adding an extra RC network at the input, and its stopband slope is twice that of the first-order filter.
wrong: In the active low-pass filter, the capacitor is placed in series with R1 at the input.
The DC gain of the active low-pass filter is +R2/R1.
At high frequencies, the gain of the active low-pass filter keeps increasing.
The second-order low-pass filter has the same stopband slope as the first-order one.
The -3 dB point of the active low-pass filter is set by the input RC network.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the active high-pass filter are correct?
correct: Technically, there is no real active high-pass filter, because the maximum passband frequency response of an active high-pass is limited by the characteristics of the operational amplifier used.
A first-order active high-pass filter attenuates low frequencies and passes high-frequency signals.
A first-order active high-pass consists purely and simply of a passive filter section followed by a non-inverting operational amplifier.
The frequency response is the same as the passive filter, except the signal amplitude is increased by the amplifier gain.
Higher-order active filters are formed by cascading first and second order filters; an odd order starts with a first-order filter at the input.
wrong: The maximum passband response of an active high-pass filter is infinite.
A first-order active high-pass consists of a passive low-pass section followed by an inverting amplifier.
The active high-pass attenuates the signal amplitude compared to the passive version.
An even order filter starts with a first-order stage.
Cascading stages decreases the overall filter order.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the active band-pass filter are correct?
correct: The cutoff frequency of the low-pass part of a band-pass filter must be higher than the cutoff frequency of the high-pass part.
The bandwidth is the difference between the two -3 dB points; for cutoff points at 200 Hz and 600 Hz, the bandwidth BW = 600 - 200 = 400 Hz.
A very simple active band-pass can be made by connecting passive high-pass and low-pass filter stages to an amplifying circuit.
The first stage of the simple band-pass is the high-pass stage which uses the capacitor to block any DC bias from the source.
An IGMF (multiple feedback) band-pass design gives a high Q factor response (up to 25) with an abrupt decline on each side of its center frequency.
wrong: The low-pass cutoff must be lower than the high-pass cutoff in a band-pass filter.
For cutoff points at 200 Hz and 600 Hz, the bandwidth is 600 + 200 = 800 Hz.
The first stage of the simple band-pass is the low-pass stage.
The IGMF band-pass has a low Q factor and a wide passband.
The bandwidth is the sum of the two -3 dB points.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about filter order and frequency scaling are correct?
correct: The order of a filter depends on the number of reactive components (capacitors or inductors) in its design.
The width of the transition band depends on the filter order; for a simple first-order filter it is 20 dB/decade or 6 dB/octave.
Higher-order filters (3rd, 4th, 5th) are usually formed by cascading single first and second order filters.
If all frequency-determining resistors are equal and all capacitors are equal, the cutoff frequency for any filter order will be exactly the same.
As the filter order increases, its precision decreases: the difference between the real stopband response and the theoretical one also grows.
wrong: The filter order depends on the number of resistors only.
A first-order filter has a transition band of 40 dB/decade.
Higher-order filters are built by adding resistors in parallel.
The cutoff frequency changes with each added order even if R and C values are equal.
Precision increases as the filter order increases.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the active band-stop filter are correct?
correct: All input frequencies below 200 Hz are passed unattenuated by the low-pass filter, and all frequencies above 800 Hz are passed unattenuated by the high-pass filter.
Input signal frequencies between the two cutoff points of 200 Hz and 800 Hz are rejected by each filter, forming a notch in the output response.
It can be implemented with a single low-pass and a single high-pass filter isolated from each other by a voltage follower (Av = 1), then re-summed using a third op-amp connected as a summer.

If the feedback resistor and the two input resistors of the summing amplifier all have the same value (e.g. 10 kΩ), the inverting summer provides an algebraically correct sum of the two input signals with zero voltage gain.
A band-stop filter differs from a band-pass filter in that it rejects the band between the cutoff points instead of passing it.
wrong: Frequencies between 200 Hz and 800 Hz are passed unattenuated by the band-stop filter.
Frequencies below 200 Hz are rejected by the low-pass filter.
The low-pass and high-pass stages are connected directly without a buffer.
The summer used is a non-inverting summer with unity gain.
A band-stop filter passes the band between the cutoff points.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the notch filter are correct?
correct: A notch filter is a very selective, high-Q form that can be used to reject a single or very narrow band of frequencies rather than a whole band of different frequencies.
It can be used to reject or attenuate a specific noise-generating frequency, such as mains noise induced in a circuit with inductive loads (motors, ballast lighting), or to eliminate harmonics.
The most common notch filter design is the twin-T network.

In its basic form, the twin-T configuration consists of two RC branches in a T shape, using three resistors and three capacitors with R and C elements opposite in the T part of the design, creating a deeper notch.
In an active notch filter, the Q value is determined by the ratio of resistors R3 and R4.
wrong: A notch filter rejects a whole wide band of frequencies.
The most common notch design is the single RC network.
The twin-T network uses three resistors and three inductors.
The Q value of an active notch filter is determined by the capacitor values only.
Notch filters are used to amplify the mains frequency.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about decades, octaves and filter approximation types are correct?
correct: A decade is a tenfold increase (multiplication by 10) or decrease (division by 10) on the frequency scale; 2 to 20 Hz is one decade, 50 to 5000 Hz is two decades.
An octave is a doubling (multiplication by 2) or halving of the frequency scale; 10 to 20 Hz is one octave, 2 to 16 Hz is three octaves.
Known analog filter approximation models include Elliptical (Cauer), Butterworth, Chebyshev and Bessel.
The Butterworth filter has a maximally flat passband response and is the most often used filter.
The Bessel filter has the softest response, superior phase delay, needs the most stages and is ideal for applications needing minimal phase change.
wrong: A decade is a twofold increase on the frequency scale.
An octave is a tenfold increase on the frequency scale.
50 to 5000 Hz is one decade.
The Chebyshev filter has a perfectly flat passband with no ripple.
The Elliptic (Cauer) filter has ripple only in the stopband.

questions.question: Which of the following statements comparing the main filter topologies are correct?
correct: The Chebyshev filter is known for its rippled response, which can be in the passband (Type 1) or in the stopband (Type 2).
The ripple amplitude is directly proportional to the cutoff slope: a steeper cutoff means a larger ripple.
The Elliptic (Cauer) filter has ripple in both the passband and the stopband, and offers much better selectivity at the cost of a more complex filtering network.
The Bessel filter, despite not having a sharp cutoff, offers superior phase delay and excellent characteristics with low sensitivity to component tolerance.
The best filter depends on many weighed elements: frequency response, selectivity, complexity (number of stages) and phase delay.
wrong: The Chebyshev Type 2 ripple is in the passband.
A steeper cutoff means a smaller ripple in Chebyshev filters.
The Elliptic filter has no ripple in either band.
The Bessel filter has the sharpest cutoff of all topologies.
Filter choice depends only on the number of components.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about signal conditioning are correct?
correct: The signal characteristics include amplitude, frequency, period, phase, noise/interference (artifacts) and polarity.
The signal conditioning process includes amplification and filtering of the signal.
Signal conditioning includes analog-to-digital conversion (ADC) and digital-to-analog conversion (DAC).
Signal processing also includes isolation and securing of the signal, transmission of the signal, and monitoring and diagnosis.
The role of the ADC is to allow us to transform analog data into a digital format for further processing.
wrong: Signal conditioning consists only of amplification.
ADC converts digital signals into analog ones.
DAC converts analog signals into digital ones.
Signal noise is not a signal characteristic.
Isolation of the signal is not part of signal processing.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about ADC parameters are correct?
correct: Resolution refers to the number of bits the ADC uses to represent an analog signal, e.g. 8-bit, 12-bit or 16-bit.
Sampling rate indicates how often the ADC takes measurements from the analog signal, measured in samples/s, and is essential in capturing fast-changing signals.
ENOB (effective number of bits) represents the number of equivalent bits of the effective resolution; a 12-bit ADC may effectively be only 9.5 bits in a system.
Dynamic range indicates the interval of values the ADC can measure between its minimum and maximum level.
Latency is the time between the moment an analog signal is taken and the moment the digital result is available; small latency is crucial in real-time applications.
wrong: Resolution is measured in samples per second.
Sampling rate refers to the number of bits.
A 12-bit ADC in a system always keeps an effective resolution of exactly 12 bits.
Dynamic range is the time delay of the conversion.
Latency is irrelevant in real-time applications.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about ADC types are correct?
correct: Parallel (flash) ADCs are among the fastest and most precise, converting all bits simultaneously, and are used in real-time applications such as communication or laboratory equipment.
Successive approximation ADCs convert one bit at a time, are slower than parallel ones but can offer high precision, and are useful in measurement and control systems.
Dual-slope ADCs perform two successive approximations, one fast and one fine, and are used in medical applications such as medical imaging.
Integrating ADCs compare the analog signal with a ramp, and the time needed for the ramp to reach the signal value determines the value; used in oscilloscopes and test equipment.
Interleaved ADCs combine several ADC channels to increase the sampling rate, useful when several signals must be acquired at the same time, as in medical data acquisition systems.
wrong: Parallel ADCs convert one bit at a time and are slow.
Successive approximation ADCs are faster than parallel ones.
Dual-slope ADCs are used mainly in oscilloscopes.
Integrating ADCs are used in real-time communication equipment.
Interleaved ADCs decrease the sampling rate by combining channels.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the real-world ADC case studies are correct?
correct: For an ECG monitoring device, a 16-bit ADC with a sampling rate of at least 500 Hz is chosen to ensure precise capture of the ECG waveforms.
The low noise performance of the ECG ADC helps distinguish subtle variations in the ECG signal, making it suitable for diagnostic purposes.
For a pulse oximeter, a 12-bit ADC with a high sampling rate (1000 Hz) is chosen to capture fast changes in the pulse rate.
The pulse oximeter design focuses on low power consumption to extend battery life for portable use.
Incorrectly digitized data can lead to erroneous conclusions with potentially serious consequences for patient safety.
wrong: For ECG monitoring, an 8-bit ADC with 100 Hz sampling is sufficient.
For a pulse oximeter, a 16-bit ADC with 100 Hz sampling is chosen.
The pulse oximeter prioritizes high power consumption for accuracy.
ADC quality cannot affect diagnostic precision.
A lower sampling rate gives a more precise representation of fast-changing signals.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the DAC are correct?
correct: A DAC is an electronic device used to convert digital signals into analog signals (voltages or currents).
In an infusion pump, a high-resolution DAC is used to precisely control the drug flow rate by converting digital control signals into corresponding analog voltages that regulate the pump motor speed.
In an ECG device, DACs help produce the analog signals that create the ECG waveform.
Modern cardiac pacemakers use DACs to generate precise stimulation impulses.

DACs are used in hearing aids to convert digital audio signals into analog sound waves, in ultrasound and MRI scanners to generate waveforms, in closed-loop therapies (insulin pumps), and in calibration and testing of medical devices.
wrong: A DAC converts analog signals into digital signals.
In an infusion pump, the DAC directly drives the motor without converting to analog.
Pacemakers use ADCs to generate stimulation impulses.
DACs cannot be used for calibration of sensors.
Hearing aids use DACs to amplify digital signals directly.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about DAC types and parameters are correct?
correct: DAC types include binary weighted, R-2R ladder, voltage-output, current-output, mixed-output, voltage-scaling and current-scaling DACs.
DAC resolution refers to the number of discrete steps it can represent in its output range, expressed in bits (8, 12, 16).
The output range refers to the interval of voltages or currents the DAC can generate, defined by its minimum and maximum.
Most DACs receive digital data through a digital interface such as SPI or I2C, which allows precise control of the generated analog signal.
Errors such as offset and scale (gain) offset can affect DAC precision and must be taken into account.
wrong: DAC resolution is measured in samples per second.
All DACs use a parallel digital interface only.
The output range is irrelevant for compatibility with the connected circuit.
Voltage-scaling DAC output is inversely proportional to the digital input.
DAC errors such as offset do not affect precision.
